title: The Root of the Matter
speaker: Eileen Kiera
summary: Eileen Kiera takes up the image of roots, offering four for Buddhist practice: the intention of bodhicitta, practice, karma, and an essential rootedness. After leading a short breathing meditation with counted breaths, Eileen describes stopping at the kitchen tap to feel the water as glacier and cloud, and tracing a carved wooden chair back to the tree, the truck, and the hands that made it. The story of Shido Munan, whose room looks to a would-be thief like a giant oak, illustrates the fourth root. Eileen closes with slides of Mountain Lamp, a 114-acre practice center on a mountain lake that needs funds to build its meditation hall.

sentences.text: Well, now that everybody's settled, I wonder if everybody would like to move forward.
I invite you all to come up close so I can see you.
It's nice to see friends, new and old, up close.
I wanted to speak today about roots and rootedness.
The word root comes from the word radical.
Truly, Buddhist meditation practice is not business as usual.
Practice is a radical reimagining of our lives and of the life of the world, and I'll talk about that a little bit.
As my teacher Thich Nhat Hanh says, "Don't just do something, be there."
That's primarily what our practice is about: being here.
So I'd like to begin by giving a few instructions on meditation and spend a little bit of time, maybe five minutes, practicing meditation.
The first and foremost important thing in any kind of meditation is that your back is straight.
I noticed when I was sitting in those pews that it was almost impossible to have a straight back, because they lean back.
So if you sit forward just a little bit, and you have your feet flat on the ground, then you can be in the proper position for meditation.

It doesn't matter if you sit on a cushion on the floor, or with your legs tucked under you in seiza position, or in a chair, as long as you have those three points of contact, your legs and your buttocks.
So I'm going to sit here, and I'll ring three bells, and I'll take my timepiece with me so that we won't sit too long.
This is one of the reasons I wanted you to come forward, because now I can talk without the microphone.
In sitting meditation, we always begin with three bells.
The three bells we invite to call to us.
It's a time where we put away all the busyness of our mind, all our thinking about what we're going to do when we leave here, all our worries about what's happened in the past.
All the future and the past is put away, and we come and we rest.
It's important to have a place of focus in meditation, because if we don't, what happens is we start with a little bit of awareness, and then pretty soon we notice some thinking going on.
It's not that thinking is bad, but we lose ourselves in the thinking.
So the practice is to have a place of focus, and then when we notice that our mind is dispersed, we simply come back to our point of focus.
Today I'd like to offer you the practice of breathing meditation, using our breath as a point of focus.
First there'll be three bells, and the bells are just to listen.
If you find that there are some words going through your mind, it might help for you to say a short little poem to yourself, a short little phrase called a gatha, that goes like this:
*Listen, listen, this wonderful self, this wonderful sound brings me back to my true self.*
That cuts through the thinking, and then you can just hear the sound of the bell.
When the bell has died away, let your awareness just rest with your breathing.
I think it helps to have this place right in your belly as a place where your focus is resting, and then you breathe in and breathe out just naturally.
Everything about meditation is completely natural.
We don't force our breath to be long or to be short.
We just let our awareness rest with our natural inhalation and exhalation.
Sometimes it helps to count our breath.
It's a little bit sharper focus.
When we breathe in, we let our awareness rest in our belly, and on our exhalation we say "one," just quietly to ourselves.
On the second breath we breathe in, and on the exhalation we say "two," just quietly to ourselves.

When we notice we've been thinking, we've started thinking about, well, what's going to happen next, then we simply come back to rest in our body with this breath, breathing in, and we start over at one again.
We can count as high as ten, which, if you make it there, that's amazing.
It's not that there's anything wrong with thinking.
It's just remembering to come back to being present to your body, to resting in your body, and to this gentle, natural in and out flowing of your breathing, your life force.
So we'll begin with three bells and then we'll end with one bell.
To the person on your right and then to the person on your left.
Find out their name, and a simple act is a practice of the first root of our tradition.
That is stopping enough to look inside and finding our deepest intention in our lives.
We stop our busyness.
We stop all our planning and all our worrying.
We just get quiet inside.
We see that there is a really deep [unclear: "for"] there to be goodness and peace manifest in the world.

When I spoke about our practice being a radical reimagining of our lives and of the life of the world, it is so that that peace, that desire for peace, that expression of kindness in the world be manifest, and that we be the manifestation of that.
It's like taking a seed and planting it in the ground.
This intention of ours for the world to be a place of goodness and compassion, and for us to be a manifestation of that in the world, that deep intention is a seed.
When we plant it in the ground and we remember that it's there, then we come back to touch it every day.
It's like once we've planted our garden, we have to come back.
We don't have to do anything to make the seed grow particularly, but we need to give it some water, pull the weeds around it, maybe protect it sometimes from too much sun or cold at night.
It's like that in our own being, that deep desire for compassion to be manifest in the world, for peace to be the way of our lives.
If we touch that intention every day, then it begins to grow and we begin to find ways for that to become the way we live our lives.
It's a deep desire to help in the world.
In Buddhism, we call it bodhicitta, the desire to wake up, the desire to be here for the sake, for the good of all, everybody.
This first root is where our practice begins in Buddhism.
When we've touched that desire within ourselves, then we want to find ways to make it manifest in the phenomenal world, and that becomes our practice.
Our practice then is the second root in Buddhism.
Practice is manifest in a couple of different ways.
First of all, meditation, as we just practiced it a few minutes ago, is really a foundation to having this seed begin to grow.

We need to take time out of the busyness of our lives and the constant thinking that goes on, the constant drive to be getting things done, our projects, our constant worry about what's been in the past, what's happened to us, what's happened to other people, or even getting lost in the present, being distracted all the time.
By having a meditation practice, we make a commitment to ourselves to take a few minutes every day just to be, to be still and to be present.
It's a kind of renewal.
It's a wonderful, refreshing practice, coming back and just letting ourselves be present in the world.
As I said, in meditation it's often difficult to do that because our mind is habituated to being busy.
To come back to ourselves and rest in our body and rest in our breath often requires a little bit of discipline.
When you hear the word discipline, lots of people have a reaction: "Oh, discipline."
But actually the word discipline comes from the word disciple, and the word disciple comes from the word love.
When we sit on the cushion, it's a practice of love.
It's a practice of creating a space for what is most naturally true about us to arise, our own goodness.
Without the stillness of a meditation practice, it gets buried.
With all the demands on us, with all the hard news that we're constantly bombarded with, it's hard to find that place of stillness where we can touch what is more deeply true about our lives.
I always recommend that everyone has a practice of meditation, even if it's only for five minutes a day, to take time out of your busy life to stop and to rest in your body and rest in your breath.
In our tradition, we also have a practice of listening.
When I introduced the bell, I introduced a short phrase that you can say to help you listen well when there's a bell.
Listening also can happen throughout the day, and this is where our meditation practice begins to come off the cushion and start to live and inform our daily lives.
We call this the practice of mindfulness.
It's a wonderful practice because nobody knows your practice.
It's just something you can do for yourself.
But when you do it for yourself, you do it for all beings.
Walking down the street, when we let go of all our rushing about, we're not planning, and we just touch the earth with our feet.
It's a wonderful practice in the fall with the leaves crunching.
We touch the earth, we hear the sounds of the leaves falling, crunching under our feet, and we let all worry, all anxiety, all our projects fall away.
We're just present here in the beauty of deeply nourishing practice.
It's really nice to have listening as a practice.
One of my personal practices is that every morning, the first words I hear, I stop and I listen well, because I know they come from the person I love best in the world.
I touch that person in my heart.
The sound of the bell, the voice of the person we love the best, the falling leaves, rushing water: all are beautiful sounds.
When we stop and put aside our busyness so that we can touch those sounds and be touched by them, we become bigger.
We include more.
It's really important in our practice of meditation and mindfulness to make it personal.
Jack Duffy Roshi, my husband, speaks about becoming porous in the world so that we hear the call of the varied thrush as the morning light slips over the mountains.
That song of the bird is a song of our own heart.
The smile of our beloved over a steaming bowl of oatmeal in the morning as we sit at the table together.
In this way, all things become our teacher, our daughter crying, "Mommy, mommy."
Immediately, we are there.
So whatever we have at hand, we give ourselves fully to it.
This is something we can do every moment, every day.
It's a practice of mindfulness, and it complements our sitting meditation on the cushion.

I always recommend to people to find two or three things they do during the day where they will remember to stop, to breathe in, breathe out, put aside all their busyness, and to be completely present to it.
One of the practices I found very helpful is whenever I turn on the water.
And I turn on the water a lot.
I turn on the water to do the dishes.
I turn on the water to brush my teeth.
I turn on the water to do laundry, wash my hands for the pets.
So often we turn on the water.
Whenever I turn on the tap, I stop and I think about that water.
I think about how that water has come to me freely, the water that comes from the mountains, the glaciers.
When I stop and I touch that water or I take a drink of water, how delicious, how wonderful.
I know that the universe is becoming me in that moment, that I am truly not separate from the ocean, the clouds, the rain.
In practice, we become very big.
We include all things.
We become aware that we're really not separate from anything in the world.
This is very deeply nourishing, because the universe is pouring itself forth for our sake every moment.
When the sun shines on us, we feel the warmth on our skin.
It's a lovely part of walking meditation, to be so aware that we feel the cool breezes on our cheek and the warmth of the sun on our back.
How wonderful it is.
The sun, we know scientifically, is helping us create vitamin D.
We know scientifically also that when we take food and we eat our food, we're also eating the sun and the rain.
All of the universe is being embodied.
How generous the universe is.
That brings up for me the third root of understanding in Buddhism, and that is the root of karma.
Karma is understood in a lot of different ways.
Sometimes as cause and effect.
Everything we do creates the next moment.
And yet there's something more about karma.
Each and every one of us is really special and unique, and our lives are unfolding in a special and unique way.
There has never been anyone like you ever before on earth.
And the universe must want you here.
When we begin to realize and value ourselves as that unique expression of the whole universe, of the earth, the sky, the sun, then we begin also to see and value other people in that way.
A unique and special manifestation.
Nobody has the same story as you have.
Nobody was born in the same way of the same parents.
Nobody has the same look.
Each and every person.
Each and everything: unique and special, and unfolding.
Not solid, in the sense of unchanging.
Sometimes we'd like it to be that way.
If life was unchanging, then our children would never grow up, and the sunflower seeds that we planted would never turn into a flower and into seed for the birds.
Everything is profoundly interconnected, unfolding, and yet at the same time unique and special.
There is an intimacy in all existence.
Everything depends upon everything else.
And when we begin to realize that, then our intention, our first root, begins to grow much stronger.
We realize that when we speak with someone in kindness, we create a field of kindness in the world.
When we reach out to someone in love, we create a field of love in the world.
And it is a sacred duty.
And then there's something else about this whole matter of karma: it's not fixed.
We are constantly being created and constantly creating others.
We have a choice.
The seed that we plant is what ripens in our lives and in the world.
So it's important to know our own special tendencies: places where we get caught or where anger arises, places where we are aware that we soften and our heart opens.
Then we make choices that lessen the suffering.
In that choice we create more suffering or we create less.
We lessen it.
So it's really important, when we begin a practice of meditation, that we really are very much looking at ourselves, just making it personal.
And it's important that we don't get lost in our sense of inadequacy, in our self-judgment, in the places we feel we fail.
We simply are aware of those things and then make a different choice the next time.
But it takes this awareness.
It takes this acknowledgement of when I act this way, of my partner, when someone treats me this way, I suffer.
And to be aware of where those places of joy and suffering exist.
Now, this takes knowing what we are about and knowing our mind.
And very much meditation is becoming aware and getting to know our mind and how our mind works.
It's not particularly, or specifically, Buddhist practice is not about self-improvement.
But in our practice we see where we get stuck in smallness and cut-offness.
When we are aware of that, where our heart closes, then we can make the choice to just let go of that.
And bit by bit we are transformed.
Specifically, our practice is, as Dogen said, to study the mind in order to know the mind.
To know the mind, all things come forth in complete intimacy.
We forget ourselves in the act of uniting with something.
When we are walking down the street in mindful walking and are aware of the warmth of the sun on our back, we forget all about ourselves, our past, our future.
We are embraced by the gift of the warm sun.
It's important to remember to practice in ways that we are nourished by the universe, where we touch our natural nourishment of the universe.
I spoke about turning on the water and realizing our deep interconnectedness with water.
If we look at anything in our lives and we look carefully, we see that everything is there.
When we look at a chair in our living room, we have a very beautiful wooden chair that has some hand carvings on it.
I think it's probably from Scandinavia.
When I look at that chair, I can see that there once was a tree that this chair came from.
In order for the tree to be this beautiful chair, somebody's hands worked to take the tree down, to shape it, to form it, to put it together.
That's how that chair got [unclear: "got"].
In the chair also is the truck that carried it, the oil and the gas that propelled the truck.
It also is the work of my own hands, the money that I earned in order to be able to pay for that chair.
If we look even further back into the tree, we'll see the tree, of course, exists because the earth is here, because the sun is here.
The tree also exists because we are breathing, because the tree breathes in what we breathe out, and we breathe in what the tree breathes out.
So intimate is our deep connect.
We can remember to look at the world in this way every day.
Actually, I spoke about this being a radical practice, and I think this is a radical practice because it really addresses where we tend to get lost and caught up in our mind.
So much of the outward focus that is happening in the world is on what's wrong, on the inadequacies.
Again, that's reflected in our own lives.
It's important that we are aware when we have thoughts of judgment, anger, and sense of inadequacy, and not get caught up in that, not have that be the only basis for our life.

If the Buddha had gotten lost in self-judgment or in his inadequacies and regrets, instead of taking up the question of the suffering of the world, he would never have realized that everything is okay from the very beginning.
Important realization.
And that calls up the fourth root of our practice, which is our essential rootedness.
Robert Aitken Roshi calls that the original dwelling place.
There's a story, an old Japanese story, about a monk named Shido Munan.
For those of you who have studied a little bit of Buddhism, he was the grandfather of Hakuin Zenji.
Shido Munan was returning to his home with a great deal of gold that had been given to him to build a new monastery.
There was a very wily thief who was able to tell when someone was carrying a great deal of wealth with them.
So he followed Munan as he was walking back to his home.

It was a few-day travel, and at the first night where he stayed at an inn, the bandit also, the thief also, checked into that inn, thinking that he would, in the middle of the night, go into the room and steal the gold from Munan.

And so the night began to pass, and the bandit went to Munan's room, opened the door, and was totally taken aback, because what he saw in the room was a giant oak tree with roots that went deep, deep into the earth and branches and leaves that were pressing at the ceiling and the walls.
He was so shocked and surprised that he immediately closed the door and left.

The next morning the bandit came up to Munan and said, "I am one of the greatest thieves of all time, so I always know when someone's carrying a lot of wealth with them, and so wily that I can take that wealth from them without them ever knowing they've lost anything.
But last night I met someone who was greater than me, who had greater skill than me.
You, who are so deeply rooted that you appear as a great tree."
And the bandit relinquished his ways of thieving and became a disciple of Munan and was said to have become a very good student.
Many of you have seen movies or have been at a retreat with the Venerable Thich Nhat Hanh.
You know what it is to be able to walk like a tree, to move like a mountain.
In his presence you have the sense of everything stepping forward with him.
You are pulled along.
And that is very much a fruit, as well as the root of our practice, that we are so present, all is embodied.
This is the great intimacy, our essential root as a part of the unfolding nature of the universe.

Our thoughts and fears, the ways we fix our mind on our inadequacies or the inadequacies of people around us, or the situation, the circumstances in our life or the world, they keep us cut off from realizing this intimacy.
When we pay attention, we notice when we are losing ourselves, and remember to come back to the present moment.
We pay attention in each moment the way we pay attention to someone we love.
We pay attention the way a mother pays attention to her baby.
Embrace this moment with our loving attention.
And we begin to truly live life as it is, unfolding only in this moment, not in the past, not in the future.
Life as it is in this moment, opening and passing away, is much easier.
It is the ease of our moment-by-moment life, and also the great ease that is revealed in the intimacy with the root of the matter.
Nagarjuna said, "Clinging is to insist on being someone.
Not to cling is to be free to be no one."
The freedom of the earth unfolding, embodied in our bodies.
Now, in order to practice meditation and mindfulness, it's important that we have a structure.
It's very difficult, I think almost impossible for most people, to be able to practice without having a particular form of practice.
And so we have sitting meditation.
We have the form of walking meditation, which I talked very briefly about.
We have the form of listening to the sound of the bell.
We have the form of following our breath.
All forms that help us remember to come back, to be present, to experience what's here in this moment and not be lost, thinking about the past, dwelling in the future.
Another kind of structure is also really important for our practice to take root in this country, in this nation.
The practice of Buddhism has come from many different Asian countries.

Those of you who are attending all the talks in this series, there is a talk being given from someone who's practicing in the Tibetan tradition, and someone who's been practicing in a tradition that comes from Japan, someone who's practicing in a tradition that comes from Thailand, all these different traditions.
Something very interesting has happened.
All those traditions began in one place in India with the Buddha, a human like you and I.
And then those teachings spread across Asia to all these different countries.
In each country where Buddhism took root, it became a manifestation of the culture that existed in that nation.
For the first time in 2,500 years, Buddhism is all coming together again.
All these different expressions of the original nature are coming together again here in this country.
The new root is taking, is being formed.

And it's important, because it is important for us to be able to look at the suffering in our own hearts and minds and find ways to transform that suffering so that our deepest intention, expressing peace, kindness, and compassion in the world, can be manifest.
One of the forms that is necessary, I believe, for practice is that we have a place where we go to.

For those of you who have ever lived at a center or spent time at practice centers, you know that those centers that are dedicated to prayer, to meditation, are places of great peace. [unclear: "The air takes all meditation and prayer into a monastery somewhere"].
Only people feel it when they come to church, I believe, too.

And so it's also really important that in our Buddhist tradition we find ways of creating centers where people come and take refuge in the air, the quality of peace that is being created there, the quality of compassion.
And so a number of people have been asking me about what my husband Jack Duffy and I have been doing in terms of creating a center.
We have a rural practice center about 45 minutes east of here.
And we have a little bit of a slideshow.
Actually, it's a PowerPoint presentation to show, so that you can see this place where we are creating a Buddhist practice center.
It's called Mountain Lamp.
We have 114 acres of land.
It's on a lake in the mountains.
And we've been building this place bit by bit for almost 10 years now.

We are at the point now of building a meditation hall, and so that gets highlighted a little bit in this power presentation, because we are needing to raise some money in order to build this meditation hall.
Mostly we brought this PowerPoint, these pictures, so that you could see the place and have a sense of what we are doing out there in the county.
